tips: Text can glow and animate
Music is data, sound, and sight
Time ticks and words are multilingual
Text can respond to pointers, clicks, taps, and keys
Audiences can make choices
Audiences can chat with programs and words are shapes
Physics and gravity can make text tumble and bounce

example.phrase:
\¶@Phrase appears on stage, in any color, glow, and motion you like.¶
Phrase(
	'hello!'
	6m
	color: 🌈(60% 90 200°)
	aura: Aura(🌈(80% 80 200°) 0.3m)
	resting: Sequence.sway(8°)
)\
example.music:
\¶Music is notes on real instruments, at a tempo, in a key. The stage draws what it hears.¶
Music(
	Track([1 3 5 8 5 3] instrument: Instrument.piano)
	tempo: 120beats/min
)\
example.hello:
\¶Code can react to input like @Time, and text can be multilingual and spoken.¶
hellos: ['hello'/en 'hola'/es 'こんにちは'/ja 'habari'/sw 'नमस्ते'/hi]
hello: hellos.random() … ∆ Time(1000ms) … hellos.random()
Phrase(hello 4m)
Say(hello)\
example.keys:
\¶Code can react to pointers, keys, clicks, and taps.¶
key: Key()
click: Button()
faces: ['🙂' '😮' '😎' '🤩']
which: 1 … ∆ key | ∆ click … (which % 4) + 1
Stage([Phrase(faces[which] 5m place: Pointer() bubble: 'hi')] place: Place(0m 0m -12m))\
example.choose:
\¶Layout text and make it selectable.¶
fruit: ƒ(e•'') Phrase(e 3m name: e selectable: ⊤)
picked: Choice()
shown: '?' … ∆ picked … picked
Group(Stack(padding: 1m) [
	Phrase(shown 4m)
	Group(Row(padding: 1m) [fruit('🍎') fruit('🍐') fruit('🍒')])
])\
example.letters:
\¶Chat with programs and use the shape of fonts and symbols.¶
message: Chat()
word: 'hi' … ∆ message … message
line: Contour(word 'Noto Sans' 8m)
ticks: 0 … ∆ Time(30ms) … ticks + 1
shown: ((line.length() × ticks) ÷ 66).roundDown() + 1
dots: line.subsequence(1 shown).translate(ƒ(p) Phrase('•' place: p))
Stage(dots.add(Phrase(word 8m opacity: 15%)))\
example.pile:
\¶Text can have physics.¶
toss: ƒ(emoji•'' x•#m y•#m vx•#m/s) 
Phrase(
	emoji 2m
	place: Motion(Place(x y) Velocity(vx 0m/s))
	matter: Matter(1kg 0.55 0.06 0.5)
)
Stage(
	[
		toss('🍎' -2m 5m 2.2m/s)
		toss('🍊' 2m 7m -2.6m/s)
		toss('🍋' -1m 9m 1.4m/s)
		toss('🍇' 1.5m 11m -1.9m/s)
		toss('🫐' 0.5m 15m -1.2m/s)
		Shape(Rectangle(-4m -3m 4m -3.6m))
		Shape(Rectangle(-4.6m 4m -4m -3m))
		Shape(Rectangle(4m 4m 4.6m -3m))
	]
)\
example.listen:
\¶Code can react to the @Volume and @Pitch of your mic.¶
Phrase('📣' 1m + (Volume() × 8m) rotation: (Pitch() ÷ 1hz) × 0.1°)\
example.smile:
\¶Code can react to your @Face, and other things on @Camera.¶
Phrase(Face().smiling ? '😄 thank you!' '🙂 smile at the camera' 2m)\

language.title: Wordplay is a programming language
bullets: • Every program is an expression that becomes a value. \1 + 1\ is a program, and so is \Phrase('hi')\.
• Numbers carry units, so \1m + 1m\ is meters, and \1cat + 1dog\🪲 is a mistake @wordplay catches before it runs.
• Functions are values you can name, hand around, and call: \ƒ double(n•#) n × 2\.
• When input changes, @wordplay reevaluates your program and shows its new value. No need to respond to events.
• @wordplay finds mistakes before the program runs, and explains each problem.

multilingual.title: Wordplay is multilingual
bullets: • Every programming language feature has a name in every language, so the code reads in words you already know.

• Your own names can be multilingual too:
\cat/en, gato/es: '🐈'
Phrase(cat)\
• Text carries a language, and shows the language your audience reads: \'hello'/en'hola'/es\.
• The site itself is in 29 languages and you can choose more than one at a time; text appears in each.
• You can help translate @wordplay itself, right inside the app at <localize@://localize>.

accessible.title: Wordplay is accessible
bullets: • Anything you can do with a mouse, you can do with a keyboard.
• Screen readers describe the stage as it changes, and optional sounds mark what reevaluates, what animates, and what collides.
• You can read and write your code as blocks instead of text, and switch whenever you like.
• Motion can be slowed down, or turned off completely.
• Spoken output can be captioned on stage for anyone who can't hear it.

senses.title: Wordplay senses the world
bullets: • Time passing: \Time(1000ms)\ ticks along, and \Now()\ knows today's date in your own calendar and time zone.
• Where your audience points, what they touch, and which keys they press.
• Programs can respond to your mic: how loud it is with @Volume, what pitch with @Pitch, and what words with @Speech.
• Your audience can type in @Chat, and pick stage content with @Choice.
• Programs can respond to the beat of the music they play, with @Beat.

performs.title: Wordplay performs
bullets: • @Phrase puts words and emoji on the stage.
• @Group arranges them in rows, stacks, grids, or wherever you place them.
• @Pose and @Sequence turn, fade, scale, and move things around.
• @Say speaks text aloud instead of showing it.

• @Music plays tracks of notes on real instruments, at a tempo, in a key:
\Music(Track([1 3 5] instrument: Instrument.bell) tempo: 90beats/min)\

typography.title: Wordplay is typography
bullets: • Hundreds of faces, covering the world's writing systems.
• You can draw your <custom characters@://characters> and use them anywhere an emoji goes.
• The outline of every letter is data you can read and animate, with @Contour: \Contour('a' 'Noto Sans')\.
• Text wraps by the rules of the language it's written in.
• Right-to-left and vertical writing are laid out the way they should be.

docs.title: Wordplay explains itself
bullets: • Documentation is part of the language with @Doc, not a comment beside it.
• A searchable <guide@://guide> explains every built-in feature, with examples.
• Every mistake is explained where it happened, in your language.
• You can step through a program forwards /and/ backwards to debug what happened.
• While you step, every value is shown right in the code that made it.

sharing.title: Wordplay is for sharing
bullets: • Your projects are yours, and you decide who can see them.
• You can invite other people to build a project with you.
• <Galleries@://galleries> gather projects around a theme.
• Teachers can make classes and follow their students' work: <teach@://teach>.
• You can remix anyone's public project and make it your own.

free.title: Wordplay is free and open
bullets: • @wordplay is free and it always will be.
• It's open source: you can read how it works and you can help us change it.
• It comes from the <University of Washington@https://ischool.uw.edu/> Information School.
• There's a community of creators, teachers, and contributors.
• <Donations@://donate> pay for what it costs to run.

instructions.empty: Choose a drawing mode in the palette to create shapes.
instructions.unselected: Choose a drawing mode or select and edit shapes. Use *$control-a* to select everything and *$control-z* to undo.
instructions.selected: Use the *arrow* keys to move shapes. Hold *shift* to add more shapes to a selection. Use *delete* to remove the selection. Use *$control-c* and *$control-v* to copy and paste, and *$control-z* to undo. With one path selected, press *enter* to edit its points. Use the controls below to change the selected shapes.
instructions.eraser: To erase shapes, click or tap on them. Drag to erase pixels. Use the *arrow* keys to move the eraser and *space* to delete.
instructions.pixel: To draw pixels, choose a color. Then, click the canvas or use the *arrows* to move the cursor and *space* to create a pixel. *Double-click* to fill.
instructions.rect: To draw rectangles, choose a color and stroke. Then, click and drag, or use the *arrows* and *space* key to choose a center and size.
instructions.ellipse: To draw ellipses and circles, choose a color and stroke. Then, click and drag, or use the *arrows* and *space* key to choose a center and size.
instructions.path: Paths can be line segments, polygons, and curves. Click to start add points, or use the *arrow* keys and *space*. Press *escape* to finish the path. *delete* will remove the last point.
instructions.symbol: Choose whether to add pixels or an outline, then pick a letter, symbol, or emoji. An outline can be resized and turned without blurring; pixels can be recolored one at a time. Click or tap something you've already made to select it instead.
instructions.image: Choose an image, then choose the square of it to keep. It replaces the pixels, and sits under any shapes you've drawn. Click or tap something you've already made to select it instead.
instructions.points: *Tab* between the points of the path. Use the *arrow* keys to move the selected point, *enter* to add a point next to it, and *delete* to remove it. Use *curve* to bend the segment arriving at a point, then move its handle; *delete* on a handle straightens it again. Press *escape* when you're done.

content: Have you ever felt like coding was just for English-fluent, non-disabled Westerners who grew up with computers?
Yeah, us too.

This isn't an accident. Since the dawn of computing, programming languages have been designed and built by mostly the same group of people -- mostly white, cis, English-speaking men in academia and industry in the US and Europe, and a few incredible woman mathematicians. They did their work in a time of post-colonial, winner-take-all power, and programming languages were a key tool for securing that power.
This history has led to a vision of computation that is primarily about speed, logic, profit, and domination.

This is an injustice. Because computing, for better and worse, now undergirds daily life in visible and invisible ways, and the people who have access to create with it are the ones most like its creators. The rest of humanity remains beholden to this power, because imagining anything different requires literacy, gatekept by language barriers, accessibility barriers, economic barriers, and inequities in public education.

*Wordplay* aspires to help change this. It's a programming platform designed to be global, supporting /all/ of the world's languages, but also be /about/ the world's languages. A platform on which everyone can create, with whatever abilities they have, to share interactive content that anyone can experience. For youth and young adults who want to express themselves through interactive words, emojis, and typography, playfully and artfully. Not with the goal of getting power for themselves, but to create a computational world that recognize the incredible strength and necessity of our beautiful differences.

We're a community of designers, educators, and developers trying to bring this vision to life. We are people of color, we are trans, we are queer, we are disabled, we are immigrants, we are refugees. We're centered at the <University of Washington@https://washington.edu> <Information School@https://ischool.uw.edu/> in Seattle, Washington, USA, a place that aspires to welcome everyone and undo the ableist and racist ravages of colonialism that continue today. Making this programming language and platform is a small part of that mission, offering a glimpse of a future of computing where /everyone/ belongs.

We'd love your help. Learn <how to contribute@https://github.com/wordplaydev/wordplay/wiki/contribute>, <donate@://donate>, or track our <progress@https://github.com/amyjko/wordplay/milestones>. Write our community organizer <Amy@https://amyjko.phd> if you have questions.
Are you deciding whether *Wordplay* is okay to use in your school or district? Here's what we can and can't promise.

We are not a company. We're a community-based research project housed at a not-for-profit university, and we have no revenue. That means there are agreements we can't sign, however much we want to help. We can't promise to pay a district's legal fees if it is sued. We can't promise to fix a problem on a fixed schedule. Signing a promise we can't keep would help nobody, least of all you.

Here is what we can promise. We hold the platform to /WCAG 2.2 Level AA/ accessibility, we check it automatically on every change, and we fix what we find as quickly as a volunteer community can. We gather as little about the people who use it as we can, and we use it only to run the platform. Our <rights@://rights> page says exactly what we store, and our <source@https://github.com/wordplaydev/wordplay> is public, so you can check all of this yourself.

This platform is always changing, and so are the rules you have to follow. If there is something you need that we don't do yet, write to us at hi@wordplay.dev and tell us about it. The maintainers will read it, and we will write back.

content: These are the latest new features, improvements, and bug fixes in @wordplay. We release updates weekly on most Saturdays, unless we find an urgent bug.

prompt.login: Login to save your projects, collaborate, and share:
prompt.forgot: *Forgot your password?* Unfortunately, we cannot recover your account since we do not gather contact information.
prompt.enter: It looks like your login link came from a different browser or device. Can you enter your email again, just so we're sure it's you?
prompt.paste: Did the link open somewhere else? Installed apps sometimes open email links in a web browser instead. Copy the link from your email and paste it here to finish signing in.
prompt.play: You're logged in, we can save your projects online now! Want to create something?
prompt.passwordrule: Passwords must be at least 6 characters long; if you're not using a password manager, choose three long words you'll remember.
prompt.changeEmail: Want to change your email? Submit a new one and we'll send a confirmation to the old one.
prompt.changePassword: Want to change your password? Submit a new one and repeat it.
prompt.email: Do you have an email-only account? Login with your email, and if there is account associated with it, we'll send you an email with sign-in link. New email-only accounts are not supported, to preserve privacy.
prompt.sent: If this email is associated with an account, it will receive an email with a login link. It may take a few minutes to appear. If there is no account associated with this email, you will not receive anything.
prompt.logout: Are you using a shared device and want to keep your projects private? Logout and we'll *delete your projects* from this device, but they will be saved online.
prompt.confirm: Check your old email address to confirm your new address.
prompt.delete: Want us to forget everything you've made here? This can't be undone.
prompt.reallyDelete: Are you sure? Your account and settings will be deleted immediately and your projects will be scheduled for deletion. Collaborators on your projects will immediately lose access to them. Type your email or username to confirm that this is what you want.
prompt.name: Pick an emoji or custom character to represent yourself to others.

username.change: Your username is how other people see you, and it begins the name of every character you make. You can change it whenever you like. Your old name keeps working, so anything already pointing at your characters still finds them.
username.missing: You don't have a username yet, so other people see you as *—* and you can't make characters. Pick one and that's fixed.

save.label: Save
save.tip: Use this username from now on

signin.usesPassword: You sign in with a username and a password. If you'd rather not have a password to remember, you can switch to signing in with a link we email you — your username stays the same.
signin.usesEmail: You sign in with your email address. If you’d rather have a username and a password instead, you can switch — your username stays the same.
signin.notYet: You sign in with a username and a password. Where you live, you’re not old enough yet to use an email address here — from $date you’ll be able to switch to signing in with an emailed link instead.
signin.switched: Done. Next time, sign in with your username and your new password.

toPassword.label: Use a password instead
toPassword.tip: Switch to signing in with your username and a password

error.invalidUsername: Usernames must be at least 5 letters with no spaces.
error.unverified: We couldn't check that this is a real browser, so we stopped here. This can happen on school or work networks. Trying again won't help, but a different network or browser might. If you're at school, tell a teacher.
error.deletePartial: We removed your account's data, but couldn't finish removing your account. Please try again, or contact us if it keeps happening.
error.invalidPassword: Passwords must be at least 6 characters long.
error.wrongPassword: Not a valid username and password. Either your password is wrong, or someone else has this username.
error.tooMany: You've tried and failed to log in too many times. You'll have to wait to try again.
error.unsaved: You have changes that aren't saved online yet. If you log out now, they'll be lost from this device.

feedback.deleting: Okay, deleting your projects and settings...
feedback.match: This must match your account's username.

export.prompt: Download a copy of everything you have made. It holds your projects, characters, galleries, how-tos, kits, conversations, classes, and settings. Each project comes as a file you can open in Wordplay again. Some of it is not only yours: conversations hold what everyone said, and class lists hold other people’s names. Anyone you give the file to can read all of it, so keep it somewhere private.
export.proxy: You are looking at someone else's account, so you cannot download a copy of it.

button.tip: download a copy of everything in your account
button.label: download my archive…

export.finished: Your archive $name is ready, with $#count[$count thing|$count things] in it.
export.finishedPartial: Your archive $name is ready, with $#count[$count thing|$count things] in it, but $#missing[$missing kind|$missing kinds] could not be read.
export.failed: Your archive couldn't be made. Try again in a moment.
export.incomplete: Your archive is ready, but these could not be read, so they are not in it: $kinds
export.tooLarge: You have made more than one archive can hold. Tell us and we'll help you get it.
export.offline: Wordplay can't reach the internet, so it can't make your archive.

readme.title: Your Wordplay archive
readme.intro: This is a copy of everything in the Wordplay account $name. It was made on $date. Wordplay made it for you. Nobody else has a copy.
readme.contents: Each folder holds one kind of thing. There are folders for your projects, characters, galleries, how-tos, kits, conversations, and classes.
readme.relationships: Inside each folder, items are sorted by how you are connected to them. A folder named owner holds what you made. creator holds what you wrote or may add to. curator holds what you look after. teacher and learner hold classes. collaborator, commenter and viewer hold work that belongs to someone else.
readme.device: The device folder holds things that are only on the computer you made this archive on. It has settings that are not saved online, translations you started, and work that had not finished saving. Making an archive on another computer would not include these.
readme.formats: To open a project again, go to your projects page in Wordplay and choose "open a project file". You can also drag the .wp file onto that page. To replace a project you already have, drag the file onto it and Wordplay will ask you first.
readme.excluded: A few things are not here. Wordplay leaves out the step-by-step record of your edits, because the project already holds what those edits made. It leaves out the record of who was looking at a project. It also leaves out reports about broken rules, because those are written for the people who review them.
readme.privacy: Some of this is not only yours. A conversation holds what everyone in it said. A class holds the names of everyone in it. Anyone you give this file to can read all of it. Keep it somewhere private, and think about who else is in it before you share it.
readme.missing: Wordplay could not read some things when it made this archive. They are not here:
readme.manifest: manifest.json holds the same facts in a form a program can read. It says when this was made, how many of each thing there are, and what could not be included.
readme.contentsFiles: Every item has a .json file. That is exactly what Wordplay stores. Each project also has a .wp file. That is the project written out so you can read it and open it again.
readme.contentsAccount: account.json says who you are, when you joined, and what you are allowed to do. The self folder holds what Wordplay keeps about you: your username, how much translating you have done, any warnings you were given, and your notifications.
readme.relationshipsWords: The same word can mean two things. A creator of a gallery may add projects to it. The creator of a how-to wrote it. Each folder also has an index.json. It lists every way you are connected to each item, because more than one can be true.

prompt.create: Create an account to save your projects, collaborate with others, and share your work.
prompt.username: Usernames must be at least /5 characters/, can't be an email, and shouldn't contain your name or other identifying information.
prompt.password: Passwords must be at least /6 characters/. Type it twice and write it down somewhere secure, like a password manager. *There is no way to recover your account* if you lose it, since we do not gather contact information.
prompt.region: We ask where you live so we can follow the rules there about young people's accounts. We don't keep your answer.
prompt.birthday: We ask your birthday for the same reason. We don't keep it either — only whether you're old enough to use an email address, and when you will be.
prompt.choose: There are two ways to sign in. Pick whichever suits you.
prompt.withPassword: *A username and a password.* We won't know anything about you — but *there is no way to get your account back if you forget your password*, since we'd have no way to reach you.
prompt.withEmail: *An email address.* We email you a link each time you sign in, so there's no password to forget. We keep your address only to send those links.
prompt.tooYoung: Where you live, you need to be $#age[$age year|$age years] old to use an email address here. Until then, a username and password it is — and you can switch later.
prompt.sent: If that address can be used to sign in, a link is on its way. Check your email.

content: Hi!

Let's set some expectations about your rights and ours (also in light of policy, such as the <COPPA@https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-312> and <GDPR@https://gdpr.eu/compliance-checklist-us-companies/>).

The first thing to know is that we are not a commercial entity. We are a community-based research project housed at a not-for-profit university. Our goal is to create a platform that brings you joy and helps us make discoveries about a more equitable and just world of computing. We have no interest in making money on this platform; any money we gather (usually through public funding) is used to sustain the platform, not to enrich anyone who works on it (or contributes to it).

Because we are not seeking profit, this also means that we can't make any promises about the reliability, availability, or longevity of this platform. That said, <Amy@https://amyjko.phd> is committed long term to sustaining it, and as a tenured professor, she's got a pretty stable gig.
That brings us to *data*. Here's what we gather and store in the cloud:

• Your *projects*. We store any projects you contribute and your changes to them, unless those projects appear to have personally identifiable information such as phone numbers, email addresses, usernames, tax identifiers, or addresses.
• Your *settings*. This includes the languages you choose, your animation preferences, and your tutorial progress. Everything else is stored on your device only.

• Aggregate *activity*. We track logins and the pages you visit, but not in a way that can identify you, track you across the site, or track you across other sites. We use Google Analytics in 'consent denied' mode, which only gathers minimal non-identifiable information about page views, without storing cookies, or sending IP address information to Google. We use this aggregate information to help raise funding by reporting how much the platform is being used.

• Your *chat translations*. If you ask to read a chat in another language, we translate everyone else's messages, but never your own. Some browsers can do this translating on your device, and when yours can, nothing is sent to us. Otherwise the messages go to an AI translation service (right now that's Claude, made by Anthropic), and the translation is saved with the chat so nobody else in it has to translate the same words again. Only the people in that chat can read it.
We don't store anything else. Our <source@https://github.com/amyjko/wordplay/tree/main/src> is public, so anyone can verify this, and report any unintended tracking.
*You* own your data, not us. That means:
• You control who can access your projects. They are private by default, but you can share them with individuals, groups, or make them entirely public.
• You can fully delete any project or your own account at any time.
• You can get an export of any project or your whole account at any time.
Here's how we will and won't use your data:

• We won't share your data with anyone, unless explicitly required by law. It's always possible that your data is taken without permission (a 'data breach'). If we discover that this has happened, we will notify you that this has happened using the email you've shared with us.
• We won't contact you via your email address unless you 1) make an account change that requires us to, 2) you explicitly give us consent to reach out, or 3) in the case of data breach above.

• We may analyze projects, galleries, and how to content on the platform to understand what everyone is making and how they are making it. We may share these aggregated, anonymized insights in academic publications. We will only do this under the supervision of an institutional review board, as mandated by U.S. federal law.
Finally, a note about speech. Projects are private by default, and sharing one with specific people keeps it private. What follows is exactly who reviews what you share, depending on who can see it.

But making a project *public*, or including it in a public gallery, is a privilege. This is a platform made for love, affirmation, respect, and dignity. Therefore, we expect that none of your *public* content will:
consequences: If we find a project or gallery that violates these rules, we will warn creators before they view it, or block it from being viewed. If you repeatedly violate these rules, you'll lose the privilege of posting publicly.
warnings: Here is exactly what happens if public content of yours breaks these rules. A moderator reviews it, it stops being public, and you get a warning in your notifications saying which one it is. Anyone signed in can ask a moderator to look at public content using the report button on it.
After three warnings you can still make projects, still share them with people you choose, and still use everything else here. What you lose is the ability to make anything public.
If you think a warning was a mistake, or it was a long time ago and you'd like to share publicly again, write to hi@wordplay.dev and tell us your username and why. A person will read it.
license: One more thing about making a project *public*. Public projects are shared under the <Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike license@https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/>. That means anyone can /remix/ your public project — make their own copy of it and change it — and you can remix anyone else's.

Three things come with that license. Remixers have to credit whoever made the original. They have to share their remix under this same license, so it stays open for the next person. And they can't take a public project private to keep it to themselves.

We help with the credit part: when someone remixes a project, we remember where it came from and show a link back to it. Making a project public is how you say yes to all of this, so if you'd rather nobody remixed a project, keep it private.
research: One last choice, and it is entirely yours. We sometimes write and talk about Wordplay — in research papers, in talks, and in what we show teachers and families. We would love to show what people actually make with it, but we will not show your project unless you say we can.

Every project has a *Research* setting in its sharing options, and it starts off. Turning it on lets us show that one project as an example, without your name, your username, or anything else that says the account is yours. It is per project, so saying yes to one says nothing about the others.
You can turn it off any time. Turning it off means we stop using your project in anything new, but it can't take back something we already published or presented.
responsibility: Who reviews what you share depends on who can see it.
• *Shared with no one, or only with people you named.* Nobody reviews it. Not us, not anyone.

• *In a gallery with other people in it.* That gallery's curators review it, and the chats that go with it. This is true whether or not the gallery is public: the people in it can see your work, so someone there is responsible for it.
• *In a public gallery.* Its curators review it, and so do we, because anyone can find it.
• *Public, and not in a gallery.* We review it.
Anyone who can see something can ask for it to be reviewed, using the report button on it. We never tell the person who made it who asked.

Reporting a chat message hides it while someone looks. That happens once per message: if it's kept and someone reports it again, it stays visible while it's looked at a second time. You can always see your own words.
A decision says which of the rules above it found were broken, and can carry a note from whoever decided. You'll get both in your notifications.
A gallery curator's decision applies to their gallery. It is not one of the warnings below, and it can never cost you the ability to share publicly.

content: @wordplay is a free, community-based project supported by the <University of Washington@https://washington.edu>. We rely on gifts from people who believe in our mission of accessible, language-inclusive, educational programming languages.
Here are our current costs:
• We compensate University of Washington undergraduates, especially those who are disabled or whose first language was not English, to evolve and maintain the project. This is about 90% of our costs.
• We give stipends to teachers who we collaborate with to develop multilingual, accessible curricula.
• We pay Google for <Firebase@https://firebase.google.com/> bandwidth and storage, and <Workspace@https://workspace.google.com/> services.
• We pay <Squarespace@https://www.squarespace.com/> annually for the domain.

Our current costs, assuming 5 undergraduates at $$20 USD//hour, 10 hours//week during the academic year (36 weeks) and 2 undergraduates during the summer (12 weeks), plus cloud services, are about $$60K USD per year.
If 2,400 people gave $$25 USD per year, that would cover our current costs, with any excess going to compensate more students and teachers.

design.description: This is a reference for @wordplay's visual design system, including colors, fonts, spacing, and reusable components. See the <design wiki@https://github.com/wordplaydev/wordplay/wiki/design> and <develop wiki@https://github.com/wordplaydev/wordplay/wiki/develop> guides for contributing.
accessibilityRules: Anything rendered as *text* must use one of the AA text variants (*--color-gold-text*, *--color-grey-text*, *--color-blue-text*, *--color-orange-text*, or a semantic variable that points at one), which meet the 4.5:1 contrast that <WCAG 2.2@https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/> requires. The brighter brand hues are only for backgrounds, borders, and highlights, which need 3:1 or nothing. These ratios are enforced by unit tests and by automated scans of every page, in both light and dark mode. One deliberate exception: the light-mode border grey is below 3:1, because borders here are decorative separation and every essential boundary carries another cue.

Never convey meaning by color alone: pair every color-coded state with a second cue — a shape, a line style, a glyph, or a word. For example, the editor draws the caret's highlight and major conflicts *solid*, selected output *dashed*, and minor conflicts *dotted*, so severity and selection remain distinct without hue.
See the <design wiki@https://github.com/wordplaydev/wordplay/wiki/design> guide for the full contributor guidance.
logoDescription: The Wordplay logo is a speech bubble holding one letter: a tiny stage on which the bubble can say anything — a letter of the reader's writing system, an emoji, or a circle, triangle, and square while something loads. In the app, the letter follows your primary language's writing system; on script-neutral surfaces like the browser icon and share images, the bubble shows the three shapes, about to make something.

The drawing itself never depicts motion. Movement is behavioral — the landing page cycles what the bubble says in step with the language chooser, and while loading the shapes take turns hopping, like a crowd doing the wave — and always scales with the animation speed setting, stopping entirely when animation is off.
The mark is always drawn in the current text color, so wherever text meets contrast requirements, the logo does too.

proxy.prompt:
Open Wordplay as another creator, to see what they see when something isn't working for them. It's read only: nothing you do is saved, and they won't see that you were there. It opens in a new tab, and closing that tab ends it.

Every time anyone does this, it's recorded.
